<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does useful forensic work, and most of its numbers check out. Its attrition finding is a real contribution. But its central conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," isn't supported by its own analysis. It also leaves out the strongest evidence against that conclusion, which comes from the trial it relies on elsewhere.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Reported | Computed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 98.7 / 0.800 | +23.4% | +23.4% | ✓ |
| 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% | +18.9% | ✓ |
| 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% | +14.6% | ✓ |
| 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% | +10.8% | ✓ |
| Hours 40.3 → 34.6 | −14.1% | −14.1% | ✓ |
| Hours 40.4 → 34.8 | −13.9% | −13.9% | ✓ |
| Real revenue, 1.014 / 1.041 | ≈ −2.6% | −2.6% | ✓ |
| Hours decomposition (§3) | sums to 34.6 | ≈ 36.4–36.6 | ✗ |
| Energy returns to baseline (§6) | ~month 10 | ~month 8.7 | ✗ |

**Hours decomposition.** Four days at 8 hours plus 0.7 extra is 34.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. Starting from the baseline daily average of 8.06 hours gives about 36.6. The reported total implies only about 0.25 extra hours per day. Either the per-day figure or the total is wrong.

**Energy extrapolation.** Energy fell 0.32 SD over three months, about 0.107 SD per month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 SD is gone in about 2.7 months, so around month 8.7, not month 10. The difference is small, but it is the comment's own extrapolation.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence

**The abstract claims a correction it doesn't make.** It says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. But Table 2 corrects only the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition is documented in §1 but never corrected or bounded. So the 10.8% still comes from survivors only.

**The leftover gain isn't explained by measurement or selection.** After the corrections, roughly 11% remains. The comment then attributes it to novelty by argument, without evidence, and states that "the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter." A residual you can't rule out is not a residual shown to be an artifact. "In our assessment" doesn't change what "entirely" claims.

**It ignores the Varden case-processing result.** The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature," but never mentions Varden's other stratum. Case-processing used the same randomisation, timesheets and administrative output. It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months. That result rules out the selection and measurement explanations by design.

- Novelty is the only explanation left for Varden's case-processing result, and nine months is already past the comment's own extrapolated zero point.
- The corrected Halden figure (10.8%) and Varden's case-processing figure (12.5%) agree closely despite different methods and settings. That agreement points toward a modest real effect in work not tied to presence, not toward zero.

**It generalises beyond its data.** The Data Note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The abstract and conclusion then extend the finding to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general. One pilot's non-random subsets can't support that.

## 2. Table 2 mixes corrections with changes of sample

Each row uses a different subset: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. So the fall from 23.4% to 10.8% combines two things: the effect of the corrections, and differences between which organisations are included. Presenting the rows as "successive corrections" implies only the first.

The fix is straightforward with the microdata. Compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations. Then the contribution of each correction is separated from the change in composition.

## 3. The novelty argument has untested links and an available test

- **It uses two points of self-reported energy and assumes a straight-line decline.** The decline could as easily level off at a positive value.
- **It assumes energy drives output.** That link is never shown. The Varden trial points to removing meetings as an alternative mechanism that wouldn't fade with enthusiasm.
- **The direct test is already in the data.** The Halden output index was completed **monthly**, and the authors hold the microdata. If novelty explains the gain, output per hour should rise early and fall over months four to six. Showing that trend, ideally on record-based data, would be far stronger than extrapolating survey energy. Not showing it is a notable omission.

## 4. Scepticism is applied unevenly

**§7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis.**
- The seven offices weren't "selected for analysis after the results were known." They are all the treated offices in a pre-registered stratum.
- The meetings data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- Varden's authors already labelled the analysis exploratory, stated its weaknesses, and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment's warning against citing it as an established mechanism is reasonable. Its account of how the analysis was done is not accurate.

**Weak evidence is accepted when it supports the comment's case.** The comment dismisses an n = 7 correlation, while relying on:
- three retail organisations with records;
- a two-point straight-line extrapolation;
- a novelty explanation that is itself proposed after the fact.

**The retail comparison mixes study designs.** Halden's −11.2% is a before-after change in three organisations with no control. Varden's −11.4% is a difference-in-differences against randomised controls. The similar numbers are a coincidence of magnitude, not a replication.

## 5. Record-based output is not automatically the true measure

The 19-of-23 pattern makes manager optimism plausible, and the point is fair. But the records include **billable hours delivered**. In a trial that cuts hours, billable hours fall almost by definition, whatever happens to value or rates per hour. So some of the 3.8-point gap may reflect a narrow, hours-linked output measure rather than manager bias.

The authors should show the gap separately by type of record. Organisations that submitted records also aren't a random subset.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Revenue deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue; producer or sector price indices would be better. The direction of the correction is right, but "approximately 2.6%" overstates the precision. Revenue was also reported by only 52 of the 61 organisations.
- **Seasonality isn't addressed.** The pilot's output baseline was the six months immediately before, with no seasonal adjustment. This affects both the manager-reported and record-based indices, and its direction is unknown. It belongs alongside the other corrections.
- **"Four problems account for most of the gain."** Revenue isn't part of the per-hour calculation, so only three of the four problems bear on the gain.
- **Even in the counter stratum, Varden found per-hour gains.** Output per actual hour rose 6.7%, though largely through higher utilisation, with worse service. The conclusion's negative finding should be framed per employee, as Varden framed it.

## What holds up

- **The attrition finding is significant.** The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show seven of nine left after the schedule started, mostly citing workload or inability to maintain output. If confirmed, the Halden authors should respond to this.
- **Showing that manager-reported output exceeds the records** in 19 of 23 organisations is valuable.
- **The time-tracking evidence** that actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%, directly confirms the denominator concern and matches Varden's figure of 13%.
- **The recommendations are sound.** These are record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis including organisations that withdraw.

## A defensible conclusion

The data support something like this: *Correcting for manager-reported output and scheduled hours cuts the pilot's implied per-hour gain by more than half, to about 11% in the subset with usable data. Attrition probably biases this upward by an unknown amount. Whether the remainder is durable can't be determined from six months of data, but randomised evidence from case-processing work finds a gain of similar size. In work tied to presence, output per employee falls.*

That is still a strong critique of the Halden headline, without claiming more than the analysis shows.

I can draft a referee report on the comment, or sketch the bounding exercise for attrition if you'd like to see how much it could plausibly move the 10.8%.
